content: Paederus dermatitis, also known as linear dermatitis or dermatitis linearis, is a skin condition caused by contact with the hemolymph of certain rove beetles, particularly those in the genus Paederus. This condition is also referred to by various local names, such as spider-lick, whiplash dermatitis, and Nairobi fly dermatitis. The primary irritant responsible for this reaction is a toxin called pederin, although other structurally similar compounds, such as pederone and pseudopederin, may also be involved depending on the beetle species. It is important to note that the term blister beetle dermatitis is sometimes incorrectly used to describe this condition, as it more accurately refers to dermatitis caused by cantharidin from blister beetles, which belong to a different family. When pederin comes into contact with the skin, it can spread to other areas, leading to secondary lesions. A characteristic feature of this condition is the appearance of kissing or mirror-image lesions, which occur when two skin surfaces, such as the inner elbow, come into contact. Initially, contact with pederin does not produce any visible reaction. However, within 12 to 36 hours, a reddish rash (erythema) typically develops, which may progress to form blisters. The affected skin may experience irritation, crusting, and scaling, with symptoms persisting for two to three weeks. A study has shown that the most effective treatment involves a combination of topical corticosteroids, oral antihistamines, and antibiotics. The use of antibiotics is thought to be beneficial due to the potential involvement of pederin-producing bacteria contaminating the skin. Physical Examination of the Skin The clinical presentation of Paederus dermatitis is well-documented in dermatological literature, with characteristic lesions that are often linear or streak-like in appearance. These lesions are typically erythematous and may progress to blistering, scaling, and crusting over time. Geographic Distribution and Species Paederus dermatitis is caused by rove beetles from three genera within the subtribe Paederina: Paederus, Paederidus, and Megalopaederus. The irritant pederin is highly toxic and is considered more potent than cobra venom. Different species of rove beetles are responsible for this condition in various regions of the world: Paederus melampus, commonly known as the Manipal bug or Nitte Police, is found in the Indian state of Karnataka. This species was identified in a 2007 study by dermatologists from Sri Devaraj Medical College. Despite being referred to as a blister beetle in some contexts, P. melampus belongs to the family Staphylinidae, not the blister beetle family Meloidae. Paederus brasilensis, also known as El podo, is a species that causes dermatitis in South America. Another related species, Paederus columbinus, is found in Venezuela. Paederus fuscipes is a significant cause of linear dermatitis in northern Iran, where it is an urban problem in provinces along the Caspian Sea. This species also causes dermatitis in Taiwan. The Nairobi fly, which includes Paederus crebrepunctatus and Paederus sabaeus, is responsible for dermatitis in East Africa. Cases of Paederus dermatitis have also been reported in Nigeria, France, Okinawa, Australia, Malaysia, and Sri Lanka.
